_comment: What this service ran on, and what it costs to stand up again.
Nothing is provisioned. The endpoint, the template, the registry credential and the
100 GB weight volume were all deleted on 2026-08-17 at Ernest's instruction, and the
deletion was verified rather than assumed: every RunPod listing returns zero.
This file is the recipe, not an inventory. It is here because the expensive thing about
a torn-down service is not the machines, it is remembering what shape it was.

1_volume.what: A network volume, 100 GB, and the data center it lives in decides the endpoint's.
1_volume.holds: a HuggingFace cache at <volume>/see-through/hf, about 14 GB
1_volume._note: The same bytes at two paths, so HF_HOME differs between a pod and a worker. That is the detail most likely to be got wrong on the way back up.

2_weights.took: about ten minutes on a 4090 pod
2_weights._note: Weights never go in an image. An image carrying them re-downloads gigabytes into every cold worker; a volume is written once and read by all of them.

3_endpoint._note: workersMin 0 so an idle endpoint bills nothing and a job pays for its own worker. A queue endpoint rather than load-balancing: the latter caps a request at 5.5 minutes and a decomposition takes about three.

provedEndToEnd: A job reached the queue, the transport layer put it on the bus, the interactor answered,
and the reply came back as CBOR. Two jobs: one refused by the production-settings gate
naming the number it saw, one answered with the missing-weights error naming the volume
path. Both are correct behaviour of the deployed path.
Warm worker: 789 ms queue delay, 233 ms execution.
notProved: No decomposition ran through the endpoint. The engine was not wired at the time, so what
the path carried was a refusal and an error, not layers. seconds/seconds.json holds the
measurement that did produce layers, and it was taken on a pod rather than through here.
